title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment (N = 300 matched intents) to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Under a frozen protocol we used Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators (an execution-based Batfish-style validator and a lightweight graph-based static reachability analyzer) combined by logical OR, and shared_initial_candidate semantics that generated a single LLM candidate per paired intent (declared model: gpt-5-mini). The run completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300. Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). Paired risk-difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because no validator-detected violations occurred, no repair calls were invoked and the experiment cannot evaluate whether verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates. We therefore report deterministic execution accounting, a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on the undetected baseline violation rate, and artifact-grounded design lessons (generation semantics, adversary potency, verifier diversity, repair budget) to guide follow-up stress tests that exercise the repair path. All preregistration, execution, validator traces, raw responses, and analysis outputs are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises operator productivity gains but raises operational-security concerns: generated artifacts may inadvertently expand attack surface, violate access-control policies, or otherwise introduce hazardous reachability changes. Research therefore advocates constrained generation, execution oracles, and generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as mitigations. Yet there is little preregistered confirmatory evidence that placing a verifier inside a GVR loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations under adversarial inputs. We designed and preregistered a paired, N = 300 confirmatory experiment (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) to answer: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier in a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? Our contributions are: (1) a machine-readable preregistered paired design and deterministic Dockerized execution; (2) a compact technical definition of the scoring predicate and concise validator summaries; (3) deterministic execution and analysis artifacts showing a degenerate confirmatory outcome (n11 = 300) together with precise statistical bounds; and (4) artifact-grounded operational recommendations and reproducibility materials to inform stress tests that exercise repair.
sections.related_work: Three strands motivate our design. First, execution-guided generate–verify–repair architectures improve correctness for code and Infrastructure-as-Code tasks by using verifier feedback to drive repair; realized gains depend on verifier power and repair policy [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898; https://openalex.org/W7124141852]. Second, NetOps surveys and system papers document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and recommend validators, constrained generation, or human oversight to reduce operational risk [https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4404602270]. Third, emulation and testbed work demonstrates execution-based validation is practical for research-grade evaluation but cautions about external validity versus production devices and live traffic [https://openalex.org/W4406170828]. Where prior work is sparse is in preregistered paired evaluations that fix generation semantics, archive deterministic per-episode verifier traces, and quantify the model-call versus inferential-power trade-offs; our study addresses that gap.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration: The preregistration (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) specified a paired binary design with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds + 150 programmatic adversarial variants). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Confirmatory test: exact McNemar two-sided (alpha = 0.05). Prespecified CIs by bootstrap; final CI computation used 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729 (recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Sampling and deduplication followed the preregistered rules; no exclusions or technical failures occurred (analysis/missingness_summary.csv).

Operational definitions (concise and precise). Forbidden-reachability predicate: an episode is labeled violating if, after applying the generated configuration to the deterministic emulated topology, any reachability path appears that (a) is classified by the task payload or workflow policy as disallowed (for example, reachability from an untrusted/external endpoint to a protected interface listed in the task manifest, e.g., protected_interfaces = ["mgmt1"]), or (b) violates explicit intent constraints encoded in the task payload (loss of required isolation or unintended access). This predicate is evaluated over the post-configuration network state produced by deterministic validators; per-episode validator_trace entries record the evaluated reachability pairs and violation codes.

Validators (summary of detection assumptions). We used two deterministic validators combined by logical OR: (1) an execution-based Batfish-style validator that applies the generated configuration inside the Dockerized FRRouting-style emulator and computes concrete reachability under the runtime forwarding/ACL/route-policy semantics implemented in the emulator; (2) a lightweight Python graph-based static reachability analyzer that reasons over an abstracted device-and-policy graph to conservatively detect forbidden paths. The execution validator detects violations observable in the emulated forwarding plane; the static analyzer is faster and conservative for some classes of policy violations. Both validators are deterministic in our orchestration; per-episode validator_id = 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5' and validator_version = '5.0' are recorded in scoring artifacts. The logical-OR decision rule labels an episode violating if any validator reports forbidden reachability.

Adapter contract and generation semantics: To conserve provider usage we preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single LLM candidate was generated per paired intent and replayed to both arms. This contract produced model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs (execution manifest), halving potential calls relative to independent draws. The guarded arm would invoke at most one repair LLM call per pair if any validator detected forbidden reachability; repairs were therefore budgeted but only triggered by validator-detected violations. All prompts, transformation templates, seeds, and orchestration scripts are archived in the evidence bundle for auditability.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions) with completed = 600 and failed = 0. Provider-call audit under shared_initial_candidate semantics shows model_calls_used = 300 (maximum_model_calls = 600 in the contract). Representative artifact hashes for immediate verification: execution/raw_results.jsonl (sha256 = 36ea4a5dfa90384f2a388cba4f39bf193bb3c150ea22ca60957facb20ca960f1), execution/model_configuration.json (sha256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820), and provenance/master_prompt.txt (sha256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The full artifact manifest is archived in the evidence bundle.

Primary confirmatory outcome (compact): All 300 matched pairs passed the forbidden-reachability predicate in both arms. Paired contingency: n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (see Table 1). Baseline_success_rate = 1.0; guarded_success_rate = 1.0. Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the baseline violation probability of approximately 1 − 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%).

Repair and verifier concordance: Across all archived per-episode validator_trace entries no validator reported forbidden reachability for any initial candidate; therefore no repair invocation occurred and all repair_applied flags are false. Verifier_disagreement_rate between the two validators is 0 in the archived traces. Representative per-task examples (execution/responses/task-000001-*.txt and execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json) illustrate typical medium-difficulty patterns where the shared candidate matches the reference and validators report no violations.

Statistical interpretation: The observed contingency is degenerate: with zero discordant pairs the McNemar test cannot assess repair efficacy because no candidate required correction. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction target; this assumption is not met and renders the confirmatory test uninformative for the original H1. The Clopper–Pearson upper bound provides a descriptive constraint on the undetected violation rate under the current model/validator/task configuration.
sections.discussion:
Evidence-supported conclusions: Under the exact adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate), declared model (gpt-5-mini), two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, programmatic adversarial perturbations used here, and the Dockerized FRRouting-style emulator, baseline generation satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for all sampled intents. The archival artifacts (execution manifest, per-episode validator_trace, and analysis contingency) consistently support this specific statement. What is not shown: because the repair path was never invoked, the experiment provides no evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates.

Design lessons (artifact-grounded). Generation semantics matter: shared_initial_candidate reduced model calls (model_calls_used = 300) but also reduced independent-sample variability that could produce discordant violating outputs; experiments meant to exercise repair efficacy should use independent-condition generation (two LLM draws per pair) or larger repair budgets. Adversary potency matters: the programmatic adversarial variants used here did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability for this model/validator setup; stronger or targeted adversaries are required to exercise repair. Verifier diversity and oracle strength matter: combining multiple, complementary verifier families and including production-grade execution oracles increases the chance of discovering violations. Reproducibility practicality: per-episode raw responses, validator traces, provider-call audit, and analysis logs (including bootstrap parameters and seed) are archived to permit exact replay of accounting and contingency outcomes.

Threats to validity (concise, artifact-referenced). Internal validity: constrained by the shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope (execution/model_configuration.json; deterministic_reconciliation.json). Construct validity: depends on whether the forbidden-reachability predicate and the two validators model operational security risk adequately; validator assumptions and per-episode judgments are recorded in execution/scoring/*.json. External validity: tasks are synthetic and executed in Dockerized emulation; results may not generalize to diverse production devices or live traffic (execution/task_manifest.jsonl documents emulator composition). Conclusion validity: degenerate contingency violates preregistered power assumptions. All these threats and supporting artifacts are enumerated in the evidence bundle.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation. The run completed N = 300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 under shared_initial_candidate semantics and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never reported violations, the repair path was not exercised and the experiment cannot evaluate whether verifier-guided repair rescues violating outputs. The principal scientific contribution is deterministic execution accounting, a precise artifact-backed null observation for this model/validator/task configuration, and concrete, artifact-grounded recommendations for follow-up stress tests (independent draws, stronger adversaries, expanded repair budgets, multi-model and multi-oracle evaluations). We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable replication and targeted follow-up studies.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead (model_calls_used = 300) but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and the transformation logs are available in the execution manifest for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
